title_zh: 第二十二類 煉丹騙

stories.title_en: Refining Elixir in a Deep Pit, with Long Stakes Set

paragraphs.zh: 古有炼丹之说，点铁成金，盖仙方，非人世有也。世所传炼丹之术，用好纹银三两，杂诸铅、汞辰、朱砂药物在炉同炼，每次须炼四十九日。至四十日后，须两人轮番守炉，昼夜不得暂时离守。丹成，可得九两，内除三两银本，要三两买药物，每次只出三两。一年可炼四次，共可得十二两，仅足供两人食用。故真得此方者，亦不屑为。其炼出丹银，亦可经煎，每次渐渐亏少，复归于无。但此银第二次不可为银母，若再炼，须另以纹银为母。此相传真方，费心费工，甚不易为。若云游方士，托炼丹为名以行骗者，用砒霜、雄黄诸物，炒好银为灰砂，假称曰“丹头”；然后将此与好银同煎，仍煎成银，彼便道“丹药可点成银”，此个个是弄假行骗之套子。
paragraphs.en: From of old there has been talk of refining elixir, pointing iron into gold. That is an immortal recipe, not something the human world has. The elixir-refining art transmitted in the world uses three taels of good fine silver, mixed with lead, mercury, chen-cinnabar, vermilion, and other drugs, refined together in a furnace. Each time it must be refined forty-nine days. After the fortieth day, two people must take turns watching the furnace, and may not leave it even for a moment, day or night. When the elixir is done, one can get nine taels. Inside that, subtract three taels of silver capital; it takes three taels to buy the drugs; each time only three taels come out. Four times can be refined in a year, twelve taels in all, barely enough for two people’s food. So those who have truly obtained this method also do not deign to do it. The elixir-silver that is refined can also stand further firing; each time it gradually lessens, and returns again to nothing. But this silver cannot be used as mother-silver a second time. If you refine again, you must use other fine silver as the mother. This is the transmitted true method: it costs heart and labor, and is very hard to do. As for wandering recipe-men who plead elixir-refining as a name in order to swindle: they use arsenic, realgar, and such things to fry good silver into ash-sand, and falsely call it “elixir seed.” Then they fry this together with good silver, and it still fries back into silver, and they then say “the elixir drug can point into silver.” Every one of these is a setup of making falsehood and running a swindle.

paragraphs.zh: 有一道士，自称能炼丹者。先以银灰明煎出些与人看，人多疑信相半。一富人独信之，请至家炼。道士曰：“炼丹乃仙术，家中多秽浊，恐不能成。可于僻地开坑一丈四尺深，下仅可容一床一炉，在此处烧炼四十九日。一百两银母，可炼出三百两矣。”富人依言，于后门凿一坑，广八尺，深一丈四尺。道士入坑去，命用银十两买铅、汞辰、朱砂等来，先炼丹头，三日已讫。富人付银百两与炼，日吊下三餐饭与食，道人又命讨一手握的坚实圆木七只，每只三尺五寸长，作符；用大棕索一条，交横缚柴符上，日以大斧摧打柴符。富人每日往坑上看。至三十餘日，柴符渐渐打下，只有一尺在上，心料银将成矣。道士知一月之久，防守者必懈，夜以索一头系裹银药，一头系在腰，将七只长符，每二尺打一符于上，扳援而升，将银吊起，夤夜逃去。次早送饭，下无人接。以烛照之，不见道士矣。梯下看之，银都窃去，方知彼蹈符而上，明白被其窃骗也。
paragraphs.en: There was a Daoist who claimed he could refine elixir. First he openly fried some silver ash out to show people. People were mostly half doubtful, half believing. One rich man alone believed him, and invited him to his house to refine. The Daoist said, “Refining elixir is an immortal art. A house has much filth and turbidity; I fear it cannot succeed. You may open a pit in a secluded place, one zhang four chi deep, the bottom only enough to hold one bed and one furnace, and burn and refine there for forty-nine days. One hundred taels of mother-silver can be refined into three hundred taels.” The rich man followed his words, dug a pit behind the back gate, eight chi across and one zhang four chi deep. The Daoist went down into the pit, ordered ten taels of silver used to buy lead, mercury, chen-cinnabar, vermilion, and the rest, first refined the elixir seed, and finished it in three days. The rich man handed over a hundred taels of silver to refine. Each day they lowered three meals for him to eat. The Daoist also ordered seven solid round logs of a hand’s grip, each three chi five cun long, to serve as talismans; he used one thick palm-fiber rope, bound crosswise on the wooden talismans, and each day had them pounded down with a big axe. The rich man went to look at the pit every day. After thirty-odd days the wooden talismans had been gradually driven down, with only one chi still above. He figured in his heart that the silver was about to be ready. The Daoist knew that after a full month the watchers would surely slacken. At night he tied one end of a rope around the wrapped silver-and-drugs, and the other end at his waist; he took the seven long talisman-stakes, drove one in every two chi above, climbed up by them, hoisted the silver, and fled in the dead of night. The next morning when they sent food, no one below took it. They lit a candle and looked: the Daoist was gone. They put down a ladder and looked: the silver had all been stolen. Only then did they know he had stepped the talismans and gone up, and they had clearly been stolen from and swindled.

paragraphs.zh: 按：深坑煅炼，使人不疑其逃。然用符用索，已早为出坑之计。其使人不疑处，即其脱身处也。后人鉴此，尚以炼丹为可信否？
paragraphs.en: Note: Calcining in a deep pit made people not suspect he would flee. But using talisman-stakes and using a rope, he had already early made his plan for getting out of the pit. The very place that made people not suspect was his place of escape. Later people, taking warning from this: can they still take elixir-refining as something to be believed?

stories.title_en: Believing in Elixir-Refining, He Brought Harm on a Whole House

paragraphs.zh: 方士以炼丹脱剥，受骗者历来无算，故明人皆能灼见其伪，拒绝不信。有一邴道士，术极高，拐一脚，明言已得真传炼丹术，不肯轻易为人炼。其法以丹头与人，任其以铜铅同煎，皆成银。彼自用则不须炼，但随手取出，都是银。或见人疾苦者，在手掌一捻，即取银与之；或衣袖中随来，亦是银。多肯施舍与贫人，由是，人称为“半仙”。有用银器皿设盛席待之者，食毕，令取一米桶置席上，以手取银器，件件收入桶中。及看，则空桶无一物，明言我收去不还矣。人以善言求取，则云：“已在你家内原藏器之所。”视之，果在。若恶言强取，则终不见。此谓得五鬼搬运之法。如此累显奇术，皆足骇动人。
paragraphs.en: Recipe-men use elixir-refining to strip people. Those swindled have from of old been beyond counting, so clear-sighted people can all see the fraud plainly and refuse it, not believing. There was one Daoist Bing, extremely skilled in arts, lame in one foot, who openly said he had already obtained the true transmission of the elixir-refining art, and would not lightly refine for others. His method was to give people the elixir seed, and let them fry it together with copper and lead: it all became silver. When he used it himself he did not need to refine; whatever he took out by hand was all silver. Sometimes, seeing people in hardship, he would pinch once in his palm and at once take out silver and give it; or it would come along from his sleeve, and that too was silver. He was often willing to give to the poor, and from this people called him “Half Immortal.” There were those who set silver vessels and a rich feast to receive him. When the meal was done, he had them take a rice bucket and set it on the table, and with his hand took the silver vessels, piece by piece, into the bucket. When they looked, it was an empty bucket with not one thing. He said openly, “I am taking them away and not returning them.” If people asked for them back with good words, he would say, “They are already in your house, in the original place where the vessels were stored.” They looked, and indeed they were. If they demanded them back with harsh words, then they were never seen again. This was called having obtained the method of the Five Ghosts’ transport. Strange arts displayed like this again and again were all enough to startle and move people.

paragraphs.zh: 有富人尧鲁信之，延至于家，朝夕参拜，敬礼备至，愿学其术。道士安然受拜，未肯遂传之。每日坐享其敬，饮醉而睡，睡醒而游，全不以其敬礼为意。但有甚术，凡拜之者便倾心悦服，与共席饮酒，使称颂其道。尧鲁一家老幼婢仆，皆尊敬之。唯鲁妻辛氏始终不信，累劝夫宜绝此邪人。后邴道士知之，以银二钱与其家小仆，曰：“你主母梳头时，可取她梳下头发一根与我。”小仆早晨取与之。道士得此发即作法，至半上午，辛氏中心只爱与道士通，谓婢曰：“今日我心异也。”至午益甚，又曰：“今日心中大异。”至半下午，心不能自禁，明谓侍婢曰：“吾往日极恶邴道士，今日何爱他好？你看我脸上何如？”婢曰：“你似欲睡模样。”至晚饭后，辛氏思与道士云雨之意极切，只恨一家人在旁耳。又强制住，密谓婢曰：“你今须紧跟我，或入道士房去，你须打我两掌，批我面皮，切不可忘。”及上床睡后，夫已睡着，辛氏披上衣，裸下体，开门径奔道士房去。道士正在作法催符。婢急跟出，呼曰：“此道士房，不可去！”亦不应。道士语婢曰：“你外去。”以手扯辛氏。婢近前批主母两颊，亦不管；又在面上打两掌，曰：“你未穿衣。”辛氏方醒，曰：“我是梦中来，何故真身在此？喜得你唤醒也。”手携婢曰：“快和我进去，好羞人也！”入房蹴夫醒，详言其情及得婢唤醒之事。夫曰：“哪有此理？你素恶他，故装此情捏之，岂有心既欲去，又肯叫婢挽之？这假话我不信。”次日，不得已述于夫兄言之。兄命弟逐去道士，亦不听；乃往县告之。县提去打二十，又会寄棒，打亦不痛，乃以收监。道士明是空身入监，随手取出都是银。以银贿禁子，令买酒肉入监食。禁子更加奉承，思求其方。后又解府解道，各官都加责，以无甚证据，不肯置之死。后竟托分上，放出逃去，不知所往。尧鲁一家长幼，后相继疾故，盖受其术所蛊也。唯辛氏贞正，寿考无恙，总理家政，以抚幼孙之长，至九十餘岁而卒。
paragraphs.en: There was a rich man, Yao Lu, who believed him. He invited him to his house, bowed morning and night, and paid respect to the full, wishing to learn his art. The Daoist calmly accepted the bows, and was not willing to transmit it at once. Each day he sat and enjoyed the respect, drank until drunk and slept, woke and wandered, and took no notice at all of the courtesy. But he had some art: whoever bowed to him would then pour out the heart and submit, drink at the same table, and be made to praise his Way. Yao Lu’s whole house, old and young, maids and servants, all honored him. Only Lu’s wife Xin-shi never believed from first to last, and repeatedly urged her husband that he should cut off this evil man. Later Daoist Bing learned of this, gave two qian of silver to a young servant of the house, and said, “When your mistress combs her hair, you may take one hair she combs out and give it to me.” The young servant took it in the morning and gave it to him. Once the Daoist got this hair he at once worked magic. By mid-morning Xin-shi’s heart only loved to have relations with the Daoist. She said to her maid, “Today my heart is strange.” By noon it was still worse, and she said again, “Today my heart is greatly strange.” By mid-afternoon she could not restrain herself, and said openly to the attending maid, “In the past I hated Daoist Bing extremely. Why do I love him today? How does my face look to you?” The maid said, “You look as if you want to sleep.” After the evening meal Xin-shi’s thought of coupling with the Daoist was extremely keen; she only hated that the whole family was beside her. She forced it down again, and said secretly to the maid, “You must now follow me close. If I go into the Daoist’s room, you must strike my two cheeks and slap my face. You must not forget.” After they had gone to bed and her husband was already asleep, Xin-shi threw on an upper garment, left her lower body bare, opened the door, and ran straight toward the Daoist’s room. The Daoist was just then working magic and urging the talisman. The maid hurriedly followed out and called, “This is the Daoist’s room. You must not go!” There was no answer. The Daoist told the maid, “You go outside,” and pulled Xin-shi by the hand. The maid came forward and slapped her mistress’s two cheeks; she still paid no heed. She struck her face two more times and said, “You have not put on your clothes.” Xin-shi then woke and said, “I came in a dream. Why is my real body here? Luckily you woke me.” She took the maid by the hand and said, “Quick, go in with me. How shameful!” She went into the room, kicked her husband awake, and told the matter in full, including how the maid had woken her. The husband said, “How could there be such a principle? You have always hated him, so you made up this scene to frame him. How could a heart that already wanted to go also be willing to tell a maid to pull you back? I do not believe this false talk.” The next day, unable to help it, she told it to her husband’s elder brother. The elder brother ordered the younger to drive the Daoist out; he would not listen either. Then he went to the county and accused him. The county summoned him, beat him twenty strokes, and also applied further beating with the rod; the beating also did not hurt, so they put him in jail. The Daoist clearly went into jail empty-handed, and whatever he took out by hand was all silver. He used silver to bribe the jailer, and had him buy wine and meat into the jail to eat. The jailer was still more deferential, hoping to seek his method. Later he was sent on to the prefecture and the circuit. Each official added beating; because there was not much evidence, they would not put him to death. Later he in fact used connections, was released, and fled, whereabouts unknown. Yao Lu’s whole house, old and young, later died of illness one after another; they were poisoned by his arts. Only Xin-shi, chaste and upright, lived long without harm, managed the household, raised the young grandsons to adulthood, and died past ninety.

paragraphs.zh: 按：妖术之暗中，如妖狐之投媚，必心邪而后能惑。苟心正者，虽入群妖之中，妖不能害。故傅奕不信死人之咒，而胡僧自死；仲淹下信杀子之鬼，而鬼自不来。辛氏心正，虽妖人灵法，能深疑于心，蚤嘱于婢，终不受其邪淫之毒。然则法虽巧，终不及人心之正也。后遇妖人者，其牢把心而勿睬之，彼邪亦安施哉？
paragraphs.en: Note: Heterodox arts striking in the dark are like a fox-spirit throwing itself to charm: the heart must first be evil, and only then can it be confused. If the heart is upright, even if one enters a crowd of demons, the demons cannot harm. Thus Fu Yi did not believe a curse that would kill a man, and the barbarian monk died of himself; Zhongyan did not believe a ghost that would kill a son, and the ghost never came of itself. Xin-shi’s heart was upright. Though a sorcerer’s magic could deeply disturb the mind, she early instructed the maid, and in the end did not suffer the poison of his lust. So though the method was clever, it finally could not match the uprightness of the human heart. Later those who meet sorcerers: hold the heart firm and pay them no mind. How then can their evil be applied?

stories.title_en: Elixir-Refining Hard to Shake: Poison Put in the Food

paragraphs.zh: 古潭一后生丁宇弘，机关伶俐，识尽世间情伪，人不能欺。偶遇一方士，自称能炼丹。宇弘早知其伪也，欲乘此以骗方士，故诈为不知之状而琐琐问之。方士曰：“丹是仙术，古来传于善人，专以济救贫穷者。先须采药炼成丹头，后用银一钱，与丹头同煎，可得三钱；一两可得三两。”宇弘曰：“更多可炼否？”方士曰：“只要有丹头，虽一百一千皆可炼。”宇弘先用银一钱与炼。方士加丹头三分，即煎出银三钱。宇弘喜，更以一两与煎，又得银三两。宇弘益喜，请方士到家，殷勤相待。及银已费尽，又求再炼添用，陆续炼出银三十餘两。惟以好言承奉之，愿学其术，终不多出银与炼，反将方士丹头之本骗来矣。
paragraphs.en: In ancient Tan a young man, Ding Yuhong, was sharp in devices and knew thoroughly the true and false of the world; people could not deceive him. He happened to meet a recipe-man who claimed he could refine elixir. Yuhong had long known it was false. He wanted to use this to swindle the recipe-man, so he pretended not to know and asked him in fussy detail. The recipe-man said, “Elixir is an immortal art, transmitted from of old to good people, specially to succor the poor. First you must gather drugs and refine them into elixir seed. Then take one qian of silver and fry it together with the elixir seed, and you can get three qian; one tael can get three taels.” Yuhong said, “Can still more be refined?” The recipe-man said, “So long as there is elixir seed, even a hundred or a thousand can all be refined.” Yuhong first used one qian of silver to refine. The recipe-man added three fen of elixir seed, and at once fried out three qian of silver. Yuhong was pleased, and further used one tael to fry, and again got three taels of silver. Yuhong was still more pleased, invited the recipe-man to his house, and treated him with great care. When the silver had already been used up, he asked to refine again to add more for use, and in succession they refined out thirty-odd taels of silver. He only used good words to wait on him, wished to learn his art, and in the end did not put out much silver of his own to refine. Instead he cheated over the recipe-man’s own capital in elixir seed.

paragraphs.zh: 方士思家中不奈他何，故说：“吾丹头已用尽。可多带银本，出外采药，再在外大炼。”宇弘明知其引外行骗，只自思“我用心提防，彼何以骗？”更欲尽骗其身心丹头之银，乃带银五十两，与俱出外，不肯取出费用。方士叫其取银买物，宇弘曰：“丹以换银，今已成之银，何必轻用？可取丹来炼银作路费，我银留买药。”方士尽将己丹头三两，宇弘用银十两，共炼成三十两，彼此各分一半。又远行两日，寝食严防。方士无计可脱，乃背地买砒霜在身，晚又买一鲜鱼入店。宇弘往煮熟，装作两碗，方士往捧一碗在席，放毒于内。又再捧一碗，故打忿嚏，将口馋溅入鱼上。方士曰：“这碗亵渎了，我吃。”及至半夜，宇弘腹疼。延至明晓，方士往医家求止疼药，煎服愈甚。至午，宇弘发散唇裂，腹痛难当，心疑是方士投毒，哀求之曰：“吾止有银五十五两，你能救我命，尽半与你。”时弘已不能起床矣。方士取其银置己包袱内，近床以药与之曰：“吾游方人，将攒他人银。你好奸狡，反骗去我银五十两。今止多得你五两，吾自行善心，以此药与你，凭你命当生死何如。”遂负行李逃去。宇弘急命店主以药煎。有认得者曰：“此解砒霜药也。”连服几次，疼稍止。再求近店人医之，三日始得痊愈，银已全被方士夺去矣，只沿路乞食而归。
paragraphs.en: The recipe-man thought that in the house he could do nothing with him, so he said, “My elixir seed is already used up. You may bring more silver capital, go out to gather drugs, and then refine in a large way outside.” Yuhong clearly knew this was luring him out to swindle, but only thought, “I will take care to guard. How can he swindle me?” He wanted still more to cheat him of all the remaining silver in the elixir seed, so he took fifty taels of silver and went out with him, and would not take it out to spend. The recipe-man told him to take silver to buy things. Yuhong said, “Elixir is for exchanging into silver. The silver already made—why spend it lightly? You may take elixir and refine silver for travel costs. I will keep my silver to buy drugs.” The recipe-man used all his remaining three taels of elixir seed; Yuhong used ten taels of silver; together they refined it into thirty taels, and each took half. They traveled two more days. At sleep and meals Yuhong guarded strictly. The recipe-man had no plan by which to strip him, so behind his back he bought arsenic and kept it on him. That evening he also bought a fresh fish into the inn. Yuhong went and cooked it done, made up as two bowls. The recipe-man went and brought one bowl to the table, and put poison in it. Then he brought the other bowl, deliberately gave an angry sneeze, and splashed saliva onto the fish. The recipe-man said, “This bowl is defiled. I will eat it.” By midnight Yuhong had belly pain. It lasted until dawn. The recipe-man went to a doctor and asked for a pain-stopping drug; after it was decocted and taken, it grew still worse. By noon Yuhong’s lips had split and cracked, the belly pain was unbearable, and he suspected in his heart that the recipe-man had put poison. He begged him, saying, “I have only fifty-five taels of silver. If you can save my life, I will give you half of it all.” By then Hong could already not get out of bed. The recipe-man took his silver, put it in his own bundle, came near the bed, gave him a drug, and said, “I am a wandering man, meaning to gather other people’s silver. You are so cunning, and instead cheated away fifty taels of my silver. Now I only get five taels extra from you. I will of myself show a good heart and give you this drug. Whether your life is to live or die, that is as it may be.” Then he took his luggage and fled. Yuhong urgently had the innkeeper decoct the drug. Someone who recognized it said, “This is the drug that counters arsenic.” After several doses the pain slightly stopped. He further sought a doctor from people near the inn. After three days he began to recover. The silver had already all been taken by the recipe-man. He could only beg food along the road and go home.

paragraphs.zh: 按：知防炼丹，莫如宇弘。虽百计不能骗，反骗方士银本几尽，可谓巧极矣。然终被其投毒，银尽还讫，又多去五两，且几乎丧命。幸而得生，沿路乞食，亦劳且辱矣。方士炼丹，其可信哉？
paragraphs.en: Note: For knowing how to guard against elixir-refining, none was like Yuhong. Though a hundred plans could not swindle him, he instead swindled the recipe-man of nearly all his silver capital. One may call it extremely clever. Yet in the end he was poisoned: the silver was all returned, and five taels more were gone, and he nearly lost his life. Lucky to live, begging food along the road—labor and shame enough. Can a recipe-man’s elixir-refining be believed?
